# What's New in PostgreSQL 18: A DBA's Perspective. This post is maintained by Bytebase, an open-source database DevSecOps tool that can manage PostgreSQL. We will constantly update this post to include the latest Postgres 18.x releases. PostgreSQL 18 ships on September 25, 2025. The release moves on async I/O, UUIDv7, and a set of long-requested operational fixes — adding `NOT NULL` without a full table scan, virtual generated columns, `RETURNING` with `old`/`new` aliases, and a faster `pg_upgrade` path. * **PostgreSQL 18 Beta 1**: May 8, 2025. * **PostgreSQL 18 Beta 2**: July 17, 2025. * **PostgreSQL 18 Beta 3**: August 14, 2025. * **PostgreSQL 18 RC 1**: September 4, 2025. * **PostgreSQL 18 Official Release**: September 25, 2025. PostgreSQL 18 introduces an asynchronous I/O subsystem, selected by the new `io_method` server variable. **DBA Note:** Adding a `NOT NULL` on a multi-terabyte table no longer requires an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for the duration of the scan.

Sep 12, 2025·7 min read·More by this author. Sep 12, 2025·7 min read. # Get Excited About Postgres 18. Postgres 18 will be released in just a couple weeks! Here’s some details on the most important and exciting features. ## Asynchronous i/o. Postgres 18 is adding asynchronous i/o. This is also part of a bigger series of performance improvements planned for future Postgres, part of which may be multi-threading. Expect to see more on this in coming versions. When data isn’t in the shared memory buffers already, Postgres reads from disk, and I/O is needed to retrieve data. Postgres 18 will introduce asynchronous I/O, allowing workers to optimize idle time and improve system throughput by batching reads. Currently, Postgres relies on the operating system for intelligent I/O handling, expecting OS or storage read-ahead for sequential scans and using features like Linux's posix\_fadvise for other read types like Bitmap Index Scans. Additionally, a new system view, pg\_aios, will be available to provide data about the asynchronous I/O system.

content.text:
PostgreSQL 18 was officially released on **September 25, 2025**.

Here's the headline feature list — but let me flag the ones that actually live in *this* node's territory (indexes and query performance), since that's what I'm here for:

Directly relevant to indexes/query performance:
- **Skip scan on multicolumn B-tree indexes** — this is the big one. Previously, if you had an index on `(a, b)` and your query only filtered on `b` (skipping the `=` condition on `a`), Postgres often couldn't use the index efficiently. Now it can "skip" through the prefix column. This widens which queries an existing composite index can serve.
- **Asynchronous I/O (AIO)** — a new `io_method` subsystem giving up to 2–3× faster reads on read-heavy workloads, since data not in shared buffers can be fetched with batched async reads instead of blocking.
- **Cross-version planner statistics in `pg_upgrade`** — your query plans don't go cold right after a major upgrade, because stats carry over.
- **`EXPLAIN` with buffer usage** shown by default — better visibility when you're diagnosing slow queries.

The rest are more general/sibling-adjacent: virtual generated columns, UUIDv7, OAuth 2.0 auth, `RETURNING` with `OLD`/`NEW` aliases, faster `pg_upgrade`, parallel replication streaming, temporal constraints.

The skip scan one is worth dwelling on if you care about index design — it changes the old advice about column ordering in composite indexes. Want me to walk through how skip scan actually works and when it kicks in versus a plain index scan?
